title: A rate limiter as a library, and a load test that breaks it
summary: Write a small rate-limiting library with two algorithms, then load-test it until you find where it fails and say what you learned.
context: Every API team ends up with a rate limiter, and most have a story about the day it let everything through. You build one as a library other code can import, then try to break it on purpose.
The library is the smaller half. The larger half is evidence: a load test with a clear question, honest numbers, and a write-up of where the limiter stops being correct or fast.
must_have: A library with a small, documented interface: check a key against a rule (for example 100 per minute) and get back allow or deny, plus when to retry.
Two algorithms of your choice (fixed window, sliding window, token bucket, leaky bucket) behind that interface, with a note on when a team would pick each.
Correctness under concurrency in one process: a test that hammers one key from many threads or tasks and shows the limit holds.
A pluggable store: in-memory by default and a second implementation (a file or SQLite) that proves the interface is not tied to one.
A load-test script and its results: requests per second, latency percentiles, requests wrongly allowed or denied near the edge, and the point where it breaks, in a table or chart.
nice_to_have: The burst a fixed window lets through at its boundary, made visible.
Memory growth over a million distinct keys, and how you bound it.
A design note on making it work across several processes.
constraints: No paid services, APIs or accounts. Run everything on your own machine and load-test nothing you do not own.
Fictional keys and data only (user-1, user-2 and so on).
deliverables: A public repo created after you press Start, with commits spread across the window.
A README with the interface, how to run the tests and the load test, your results, and what is missing.
judge_focus: Whether the load test asks a clear question and the answer follows from the numbers.
How you found the first thing that broke, and whether you fixed it or documented it.
An interface that is small, hard to misuse, and honest about clocks and time.
A trail of commits: the simplest limiter first, then tests, then the load test shaping what you changed.
bengaluru_context: Platform and API-gateway teams at Bengaluru product and fintech companies run limiters like this in front of every public endpoint, and are judged on the day traffic doubles.
